fundamental.thesis: Kotak Mahindra Bank is one of India's largest private-sector banks, with a strong capital base (CET1 22.1%) and growing wealth and asset-management arms (customer AUM ₹8.14L cr, +8% YoY). Profit growth has picked up sharply: consolidated PAT rose 26.3% YoY to ₹5,645 cr in Q2FY27, up from +23.0% in Q1FY27 and +5.0% in Q3FY26, and standalone NII rose 16% to ₹8,459 cr. Asset quality has improved steadily, with GNPA falling from 1.39% to 1.04% over five periods and slippages down 24%, but this quarter's growth comes partly off a weak base (Q2FY26 PAT was -2.7%), and NIM fell 23bps YoY to 4.31% as costlier FCNR(B) deposits came in. On the bank yardstick (P/B plus ROE, not P/E), a P/B of 2.08x against an ROE of only 11.4-11.7% is fair, not cheap; it sits at the 86th percentile among bank peers on both P/B and forward P/E (13.6x), so it already carries a premium that its current ROE does not clearly earn. The biggest risk is margin squeeze: falling NIM, CASA slipping from 42.3% to 41.8%, a 4.52% cost of funds and an 8.1% cut to next-FY EPS estimates while 32 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower.

The unresolved critical risk is that Q2FY27 results (filed 2026-10-12, Sep quarter) are not yet extracted — this analysis is one quarter stale precisely when the stock has significantly de-rated, and the unread filing likely contains the catalyst for that weakness.

fundamental.thesis: Tech Mahindra is a tier-1 Indian IT services company with a large Communications vertical and a multi-year margin turnaround underway, aiming for a 15% EBIT margin in FY27. Q2FY27 revenue rose 15.6% YoY to ₹16,180 cr and PAT rose 33.9% to ₹1,610 cr. Growth picked up sharply from +4.2% in Q1FY27 and +8.3% in Q3FY26, but constant-currency growth was only +7.2%, so roughly half the headline jump comes from the weaker rupee. Margins are genuinely improving: PAT margin rose from 7.8% to 9.5% to 9.9% over three quarters, EBIT margin is 14.8% (up 260 bps YoY), new deal wins of $1,023M are up 25.4% YoY, and FCF of ₹2,874 cr is 2.16x PAT. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, as the IT sector card suggests. Trailing P/E is 27.8x, inside the 22–30x IT band and at P62 among peers. Forward P/E is 17.6x, right at the peer median (P50), and EV/EBITDA is 13.9x (P33). That makes it fair, not cheap. The main risk is that much of the growth and margin gain depends on the rupee and on cost cuts, while AI-driven price deflation in legacy work and weaker European auto clients cap underlying constant-currency growth.

fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. Revenue re-accelerated sharply in H1 FY27 to ₹1,45,463 cr (+12.6% YoY, with Q1FY27 at +13.9%), up from a sluggish +4.6% in FY26, and PAT margins expanded from 15.9% in Q3FY26 to 18.8% in H1 FY27 — but the critical flag is that FY26 constant-currency growth was -2.4%, meaning the INR headline re-acceleration is substantially FX-tailwind-driven (INR/USD ~94.96 vs ~84 in FY26) rather than evidence of genuine organic demand recovery; EBITDA margins have also contracted from 28.7% to 27.2%, and deferred revenue declined ₹1,092 cr QoQ, both pointing to margin and pipeline softening beneath the headline beat. At 16.3× trailing P/E — a 33.7% discount to the IT sector peer median of 24.7× and cheapest in sector on forward P/E at 13.4× — TCS screens unambiguously cheap versus both sector peers and the benchmark range of 22–30×, with a pristine balance sheet (CFO/PAT 0.94×, FCF ₹23,768 cr in H1) providing a durable floor; the P/E yardstick is used here as primary per the asset-light IT services model, and EV/EBITDA at 11.1× (P17 in sector vs median 14.7×) corroborates the cheap read. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer, with about 8.5% of organised jewellery retail through Tanishq, CaratLane and Mia, and about 27% of the analog watch market, across 3,758 stores (up from 3,400 at FY26). Growth is speeding up, not slowing as the auto-label says: Q2 FY27 revenue rose 25.1% YoY to ₹20,533 cr, against an implied ~14% in Q1. H1 FY27 revenue rose 19.1% to ₹41,970 cr, with jewellery same-store sales growth of 15% and CaratLane up 31%. H1 PAT of ₹4,170 cr (+88.6%) includes a one-off ₹671 cr fair-value gain on the Damas put option; without it PAT is about ₹3,499 cr (+58%), an 8.3% margin versus 6.3% a year ago, and FY EPS estimates are up 13.8% in 30 days. On valuation, the peer set is mostly autos, so I graded on EV/EBITDA and P/E against premium-retail norms. At 74x trailing P/E, 49x forward P/E and 48x EV/EBITDA (P94 vs peers, more than double the 21.9x median), I grade it expensive. Strong delivery and 37% ROE partly justify the premium, and 49x forward sits below the 60–100x range typical of premium consumer names. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: H1 operating cash flow was -₹11,177 cr, borrowings rose 2.5x to ₹24,265 cr and debt/equity is about 1.5. Some of this is normal gold-on-loan and inventory build, but at this price a guidance reset or a gold-price shock could cut the multiple by 25–40%.

Hindalco is India's largest integrated aluminium and copper producer. It also owns Novelis, the world's largest maker of flat-rolled aluminium, so its earnings are tied to LME metal prices, the metal spread and conversion volumes. But much of this growth comes from acquisitions (wiring harness revenue +68% after deals) while global car production fell 2.3%, and the EBITDA margin (operating profit as a share of revenue) slipped to 8.8% from 9.0% a year ago and 9.5% in FY26. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy global supplier, the stock looks cheap at 13.9x, 27% below the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x (P20 among peers). Other measures are less flattering: trailing P/E of 39.3x is above the 18–28x auto range (though forward P/E is 22.1x), P/B is 4.1x against a return on equity of only 10.1%, and the price sits at 88% of its 52-week range, so overall it is fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that buying growth through acquisitions hides weak organic demand in Europe and China while copper and aluminium cost inflation keeps squeezing margins.

By the press-release figures, Q2 revenue was ₹45,924 cr and PAT ₹4,650 cr, a margin of about 10.1%, down from 11.3% in Q1. The pre-computed trend signals mix half-year and quarter periods, so I did not rely on them. Using enterprise value to operating profit (EV/EBITDA) plus dividend yield, as the sector card advises for a volume and tariff business, valuation is fair. EV/EBITDA is 11.6x, exactly the peer median, and trailing P/E is 14.65x, at the peer median and just above the 8–14x energy range. P/B is 1.26x against an annualised H1 ROE of about 19%, which looks attractive. The forward P/E of 9.5x depends on FY27 estimates that analysts raised 28% in 30 days while trimming next-year estimates by 3.5%. The biggest risk is that the doubling of profit comes mostly from gas-marketing spreads, which swing with LNG prices and are not structural. That makes FY27 look like a peak year. The newly started Mangalore PTA plant (purified terephthalic acid, a petrochemical) also adds exposure to a segment that is currently losing money.

Zydus Lifesciences is a diversified pharma company: it sells branded medicines in India (it is outgrowing the market, with 19% growth in Q2 and share gains in cardiology, diabetology and respiratory), it is the 3rd-largest US generics player, and it has growing consumer wellness and medtech arms. Revenue grew +29.2% YoY in Q2FY27 to about ₹7,910 cr, up from +21.9% in Q1. Profit went the other way: Q2 PAT of about ₹946 cr was down 26.6% YoY (Q1 was down 35.9%), the PAT margin fell from 18.6% in FY26 to about 11.7%, and EBITDA margin dropped from 32.9% to 24.0% as depreciation (+101%) and finance costs (+85%) jumped with the investment and acquisition cycle. On the main yardstick, P/E, the stock trades at 21.7× trailing earnings, well below the 28–40× pharma range and the cheapest 8% of peers. Other measures show a smaller discount: forward P/E of 23.3× is only 9% below the peer median and higher than the trailing figure, meaning earnings are expected to fall, EV/EBITDA of 16.1× sits at P31 of peers, and the stock is at 90% of its 52-week range. Overall that is fair value rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that margins do not recover from the reset to ~24% while US growth slows to single digits, on top of the generics-tariff review and 5 FDA observations at the Moraiya plant.

fundamental.thesis: IDFC First Bank is a mid-sized private bank with a retail-heavy loan book and a strong deposit franchise (CASA 48.4%), now scaling fast after years of rebuilding profitability. In Q2FY27, PAT was ₹1,045 cr, up 196.5% YoY off a depressed base and above ₹1,000 cr for a second straight quarter. Loans grew 30.1% YoY (22.2% excluding FCNR(B)-backed loans, up from 20.6% in Q1), deposits grew 25.9%, and asset quality kept improving: net NPA fell from 0.48% to 0.44% to 0.40%, and gross NPA was 1.32% vs 1.61% at FY26-end. Valuation is graded on P/B plus ROE, as the sector card requires for lenders, not on trailing P/E: P/B is 1.31x (P36 among peers, 11% below the 1.5x median) against annualised ROE of only 10.6%, which is below the 12% bar for 'cheap', so the stock is fair. The 38x trailing P/E is distorted by weak FY26 earnings (PAT ₹1,611 cr), and the 11x forward P/E sits exactly at the peer median. The main risk is that rapid growth is outpacing the bank's profitability engine: CASA slipped from 50.8% to 48.4% and NIM was diluted by FCNR(B) funding, Q2 ROA fell to 0.93% from 1.06%, and capital adequacy (CAR) dropped to 15.05% from 15.6% while the loan book grows about 30%.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Hotels (IHCL) runs India's largest hotel chain, with Taj and other brands across 670 hotels including 280 in the pipeline. It earns more and more from asset-light management fees, which grew 25% YoY in Q2, and it is still early in a RevPAR (revenue per available room) upcycle, up 25% YoY in Q2 and 28% for full-service hotels. Q2FY27 revenue rose 21.0% YoY to ₹2,566 cr, up from +14.6% in Q1FY27. PAT rose 23.0% to ₹349 cr. Management raised full-year revenue guidance from 12-14% to 15-17%, and H1 cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 1.27x, FCF ₹546 cr). The 'contracting' margin signal mostly reflects comparing a seasonally weak Q2 against full-year figures: on a same-quarter basis the EBITDA margin (30.7%) and PAT margin (13.6%) are roughly flat to slightly up YoY. On valuation, hotels are capital-intensive, so I used EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick. At 28.2x, IHCL sits around the 61st percentile of its sector, with a trailing P/E of 44.5x (P59) and a forward P/E of 35.6x. That is fair, not cheap, for 20%+ earnings growth, and the stock sits at 38.5% of its 52-week range. Note that the snapshot's 49% dividend yield and 18.99 debt/equity look like data-unit errors, given ₹4,369 cr of gross cash. The biggest risk is that a premium-multiple discretionary stock gets de-rated in a risk-off market with crude above $100, which could squeeze travel and MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and events) demand even while operating numbers stay strong.

fundamental.thesis: Federal Bank is a mid-sized private-sector bank with a large non-resident (NRI) deposit base. fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). In H1FY27 total income grew 16.1% YoY to ₹44,333 cr and PAT grew 28.1% to ₹6,897 cr, but Q2 includes a one-off NSE listing gain of ₹1,387 cr. Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

Aurobindo Pharma is one of India's largest generic drug exporters. About 92% of its revenue comes from abroad, with the US at 44.4% and Europe at 30.8%, and it holds 747 cumulative US FDA final approvals. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹10,263 cr (+23.9% YoY) and PAT was ₹1,124 cr (+32.5% YoY). Revenue growth has sped up from +8.4% in Q3 FY26 to +6.1% in FY26, then +16.3% and +23.9%, and PAT margin has improved from about 10.4% to 11.0%. Two things temper this: EBITDA margin slipped from 23.0% to 21.0% quarter on quarter, and US revenue fell 13% in Q4 FY26, so the filings don't show whether the recent jump is organic or how long it can last. I graded valuation on peer-relative P/E and EV/EBITDA, and the stock looks cheap. Trailing P/E is 24.0x against a peer median of 36.4x (15th percentile, below the sector's 28-40x band). Forward P/E is 16.4x, P/B is 2.2x and EV/EBITDA is 12.0x, all the cheapest in the peer group. Sell-side EPS estimates have also been raised slightly over 30 and 90 days. Part of the discount is deserved: ROE is only 9.9%, and the business depends heavily on US generics. The main risks are the pending US Commerce review of tariffs on generics and any FDA inspection setback at its 30 approved plants.

Aadhar Housing Finance is a mid-sized housing finance company lending small-ticket home loans (average about ₹11.3 lakh) to lower- and middle-income borrowers through roughly 632-644 branches in 23 states, with AUM of ₹32,643 cr growing 18% YoY. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 16.8% YoY to ₹1,048 cr and PAT rose 15.7% YoY to ₹308 cr. Growth is holding steady but slowly cooling: revenue growth eased from +17.1% in Q1 to +16.8%, PAT growth slowed from +22% in FY26 to +19% in Q1 and +15.7% in Q2, and quarterly ROE slipped to 15.2% from 15.7% a year ago, even though PAT margin improved to 29.4% from 28.3%. For a lender we judge value on price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E: 2.8x book for a 15-16% ROE is fair, not cheap. The trailing P/E of 19.6x sits in the lower half of the 18-28x NBFC range, and the ranking that calls the stock cheap compares it with the whole market, not with lending peers, so we give it little weight. The forward P/E of 13.0x assumes faster earnings growth than the recent ~16% pace, and next-year estimates have been trimmed slightly (-0.9% over 90 days). The main risk is asset quality: gross bad loans rose to 1.35% from 1.08% at the end of FY26, and only about 34.5% of bad loans are covered by provisions, which leaves little cushion if more borrowers in this segment fall behind.

The dominant risk is that CC revenue growth has halved over four quarters, the 27.5% voluntary attrition rate constrains margin expansion headroom, and a 66% concentration in cyclical Banking+CMT verticals leaves earnings vulnerable to any corporate IT/BPS budget tightening.

Elgi Equipments is a leading Indian maker of air compressors, which bring in about 92% of revenue. It sells worldwide, with roughly 51% of sales from outside India, mainly North America and Europe, through 26 subsidiaries; unlike project-based industrials, it is a product business with no order book. Subtracting Q1 (₹1,062 cr revenue / ₹103 cr PAT) from H1 FY27 (₹2,196 cr / ₹232 cr) gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹1,134 cr, up roughly 17% YoY, and PAT of about ₹129 cr (11.4% margin), up only about 6% YoY. Revenue growth slowed from +22.5% in Q1 and PAT growth slowed more sharply from +20.7%, though part of the PAT gap comes from ₹11 cr of one-off restructuring charges in H1; cash conversion stays healthy at 1.05x CFO/PAT and the company holds ₹346 cr of net cash. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-goods name: at 32x (trailing P/E 44.3x, near the top of the 28–45x industrials range; forward P/E 33x) it sits at P64–P75 against the broad market and at 86% of its 52-week range, so the shares look fair to slightly rich, and the upside rests on profit growth catching up with sales again. The biggest risk is that the gap between sales and profit growth persists while the stock trades near its high.

fundamental.thesis: Redington is India's largest IT and mobility distributor, with a large Middle East/Africa and Turkey (Arena) business. It runs on very thin margins (about 1-2%), so earnings depend on volume, working-capital turns and credit discipline; it has been tagged Industrials, but the order-book yardstick does not fit a distributor. In the latest officially extracted quarter, Q1FY27, revenue grew 34.6% YoY to ₹34,922 cr and PAT grew 94.6% to ₹453 cr, up from 22.1% revenue growth in Q1FY26, with PAT margin edging up from 1.1% to 1.3%. The unverified yfinance Q2FY27 numbers (₹41,405 cr revenue, ₹541 cr PAT, roughly +42%/+39% YoY against the implied Q2FY26 base) suggest the growth continued, but that Q2 results PDF has not been extracted yet. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E because P/E means something for a profitable trading business: trailing P/E is 14.3x against a 22-30x IT benchmark and EV/EBITDA is 9.4x. Both sit around the 9th-13th percentile of the broad market, so the stock looks cheap even after a fair discount for its low-margin model, and analysts have been raising estimates (+6.7% FY EPS over 30 days). The biggest risk is cash conversion: FY26 operating cash flow covered only 0.16x of PAT, so fast revenue growth may be tying up receivables and inventory rather than producing cash.

fundamental.thesis: Great Eastern Shipping is India's largest private-sector shipping company, running crude/product tankers, dry bulk and gas carriers, plus an offshore drilling-services arm. It is net-cash (net debt/equity -0.45 per filings) and is buying back shares. H1FY27 revenue was ₹3,830 cr, up 56.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹2,578 cr, up 137.4%. Growth swung from -14.7% in H1FY26 to +56.8%, and PAT margin rose from 39.9% to 57.0%. But the derived Q2 figures (H1 minus Q1) show revenue of about ₹1,825 cr against ₹2,005 cr in Q1: still up about 47% YoY, but down sequentially, so freight rates may be past their peak. For a capital-intensive cyclical, the right yardsticks are EV/EBITDA and P/B, not the Industrials P/E range. On those it is cheap: EV/EBITDA is 4.69x against a 23.3x broad-market median, and P/B is 1.19x with an 18.8% ROE. Shipping usually trades at low multiples near the top of the cycle, though, and the forward P/E (7.17x) is above the trailing P/E (6.86x), which means earnings are expected to fall. The biggest risk is that tanker and gas-carrier rates come down from this unusually profitable stretch while H1 fleet capex of ₹1,541 cr goes into secondhand vessels bought at high prices.

Q1FY27 saw a sharp inflection: consolidated revenue accelerated to +25.0% YoY (₹1,848 cr vs ₹1,478 cr in Q1FY26, up from a steady ~12% pace through FY26), while PAT surged 91.8% YoY to ₹254 cr with EBITDA margin expanding to 23.2% from ~17.8% — the Performance & Other Chemicals segment led at +33.8% YoY, though Life Science Chemicals remained sluggish at only +4.5% YoY, a concentration risk worth watching. At trailing P/E of 28.2× (above the 12–22× Materials sector median but at P38 in the broad market, below the 35.2× broad-market median) and EV/EBITDA of 17.36× (P32 vs a 23.3× broad-market median), the stock grades as fairly valued — forward P/E of 21.47× is a meaningful discount to trailing, confirming consensus expects earnings to continue growing, and the 30/90-day EPS revision of +6.6% is supportive. Kalpataru Projects International is a diversified EPC contractor working in power transmission, buildings, water, railways and oil & gas, with 250+ projects across 75 countries. Its order book is at a record ₹71,846 cr, about 2.6× trailing revenue, and order inflows are up 60% YoY to ₹23,934 cr year-to-date. Headline revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +32.4% in Q2FY26 to +3.8% in Q1FY27 and +6.0% for H1FY27 (₹13,412 cr). Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹7,004 cr (+7.3% YoY) and PAT of about ₹291 cr (+21% YoY). Management says growth is 11% on a comparable basis after excluding the Road SPV and Brazil exits, and margins are improving: PBT margin rose 130 bps to 6.1%, and net debt fell 98% to ₹72 cr, earning an AA+ rating. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book EPC business. At 11.2× (P15 vs the broad market) with trailing P/E of 22.5× (below the 28–45× Industrials band) and forward P/E of 15.3×, the stock looks cheap. Two things soften this: the stock sits at 91% of its 52-week range, and the peer set is a broad-market fallback rather than true EPC peers. The main risk is that order inflows never turn into revenue: execution has slowed for four straight quarters while the order book keeps growing, the latest cash-flow print (Q2FY26) showed negative FCF, and current-year EPS estimates were cut 3.6% over the last 30 days.

fundamental.thesis: Gland Pharma is an injectables-focused generics and CDMO manufacturer that earns 64% of revenue from the US, and its CDMO business is now 45% of sales. In Q2 FY27 revenue grew 23.3% YoY to ₹1,834 cr and PAT grew 58.3% to ₹291 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from +6.0% in Q2 FY26 to +20-23% over the last three quarters, and PAT margin rose from 12.0% to 15.9%. Two cautions: part of the jump comes from a weak Q2 FY26 base, and Q2 slowed versus Q1, with revenue up only 2% and PAT down 8% as EBITDA margin slipped from 27.0% to 26.2%. On valuation, the pharma yardstick of trailing P/E is 35.3x, inside the 28-40x sector range, and EV/EBITDA is 20.1x, about 14% below the broad-market median. Both point to fair value, and the forward P/E of 24.1x already assumes earnings keep growing. The biggest risk is the heavy US concentration while Washington reviews tariffs on generics; meanwhile India revenue fell 42% and Rest of World fell 21%, so growth depends almost entirely on the US and CDMO. Note that several snapshot fields look wrong: a 92% dividend yield, debt/equity of 2.74 for a historically cash-rich company, and a consensus target that does not reconcile with the 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: ITC Hotels is a leading Indian luxury and upscale hotel chain, demerged from ITC, and since May 2026 has a new branded-residences arm after acquiring Kerala Luxury Resorts (Zuri) and GHK Hospitality. H1 FY27 revenue grew 20.2% YoY to ₹1,990 cr and PAT rose 44.0% to ₹385 cr, with PAT margin up to 19.3% from 16.1%; the implied Q2 FY27 alone (H1 less Q1) is about ₹1,054 cr revenue (+25% YoY) and ₹203 cr PAT, so growth sped up from Q1's +14.8%. Part of that speed-up is bought rather than organic: the core hotels segment grew 13.8%, the new residences segment added ₹109 cr, and operating cash flow is solid at 1.42x PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-heavy business, 20.8x sits about 11% below the peer median of 23.3x, P/B of 2.75x is at P30 and trailing P/E of 37x (forward 26x) is near the median, so we grade it fair with mild cheapness, and the price sits at 15% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that headline growth leans on two back-to-back acquisitions whose fair values are still provisional, while capex has nearly tripled to 22% of revenue as rising crude and a risk-off macro weigh on discretionary travel demand.

fundamental.thesis: LT Foods is a mid-cap food company tagged FMCG, and its results show fast sales growth on thin margins (about 11% EBITDA and under 6% PAT). Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, with P/E as a cross-check, the stock looks cheap at 10.4x EV/EBITDA (P11, 55% below the median) and 21.5x trailing P/E (P24, below the 40-60x FMCG range), although the comparison set is the broad market rather than close peers, and 13.3x forward P/E implies about 60% EPS growth that recent profit growth does not support. Grid connection delays (substations delivered on time only 60% of the time, about 6 months late on average) or higher interest rates could hold back the earnings ramp.

The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: Tejas Networks (Tata group) makes telecom network equipment, mainly optical, broadband and 4G/5G radio gear sold to carriers like BSNL. fundamental.thesis: Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. fundamental.thesis: ICICI Bank is India's second-largest private-sector bank, with a large retail and business-banking franchise and subsidiaries in life and general insurance. Bharti Airtel is the number-two player in India's consolidated telecom market (behind Jio, ahead of a weakened Vi) and earns most of its value from raising revenue per user, with extra growth from Airtel Africa, home broadband and Airtel Money. In the latest quarter (Q2 FY27) the filing shows revenue up 16.7% YoY and PAT up 30.8% YoY, with an EBITDA margin of 57.9% and a PAT margin of 14.6%. However, the most important number, mobile ARPU, rose only 5.9% YoY to ₹271 (₹257 in Q4 FY26), which suggests no new tariff hike yet. The revenue figures are hard to trust: the Q2 total of ₹6,088 cr does not line up with ₹21,097 cr for Q4 FY26 or ₹211,000 cr for FY26, so the 'decelerating' and 'contracting' trend signals compare mismatched numbers and should be ignored. On EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for this capital-heavy business, the stock trades at 10.5x, in the middle of the 9–12x norm for Indian mobile, so it is fair rather than cheap. Trailing P/E of 40.7x also sits inside the 35–60x telecom range, and forward P/E of 21.6x implies earnings growth. The balance sheet looks healthy, with net debt at 1.18x EBITDA, interest coverage of 7.9x and ROE of 19.4%, and the stock is near its 52-week low (15% of range), which makes entry less risky. The main risk is that the next tariff hike keeps getting pushed back, so ARPU growth stalls in single digits. Slight downward trims to sell-side EPS estimates (-0.1% to -0.3%) despite 32 of 34 analysts rating it a buy point the same way.

Comparing like-for-like quarters, revenue growth has accelerated from +14.3% (Q3FY26) to +19.5% (Q1FY27) to +34.6% in Q2FY27 at Rs 6,417 cr, but PAT grew only +11.4% to Rs 353 cr (5.5% margin) and H1 PAT fell 4.0%. Contribution margin compressed from 20.1% to 18.2%, cables margin fell from 17.7% to 13.9% on aluminium volatility, and Q2 CFO was negative (-0.45x PAT, FCF Rs -814 cr) due to cables inventory build and stepped-up capex. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA against the actual peer set (which is industrials-heavy, so the card's 60-100x consumer multiples do not fit cleanly), trailing P/E of 42.4x sits at P31, about 21% below the 53.8x peer median, while forward P/E of 33.5x and EV/EBITDA of 33.1x are roughly at median, so the stock is fair rather than cheap. The near-52-week-low position reflects falling FY-EPS estimates (-5.3% over 30 days) and the President's resignation on 2026-10-27.

fundamental.thesis: ICICIPRULI (now ICICI Life Insurance) is one of India's largest private life insurers, with ₹3.29 lakh cr of assets under management, a 229.9% solvency ratio and a 99.3% claim-settlement ratio. New business has picked up after a flat FY26: in H1FY27, annualised premium equivalent (APE) grew +15.1% YoY to ₹4,935 cr (FY26 was only +2.2%), retail APE recovered from -0.1% to +9.9%, VNB grew +22.3% to ₹1,283 cr, and VNB margin widened to 26.0% from 24.7% in FY26. Gross premium grew +15.3% to ₹24,505 cr and PAT +26.5% to ₹760 cr, but PAT is not the right yardstick for a life insurer. On the life-insurer yardstick, price to embedded value (P/EV), the stock trades at about 1.24x (₹70,497 cr market cap vs ₹56,669 cr EV, which grew +12.2% YoY; FY26 return on EV was 11.9%), which looks cheap. Peer ranks agree: P25 on P/B and forward P/E, at a 22–25% discount to the peer median. The biggest risk is growth fading: management has guided that protection growth will cool from the 40–50% pace of the last four quarters, and Prudential's pending reclassification from promoter to investor could mean an overhang of stake sales, while the market is in a RISK_OFF regime.

Bajaj Holdings is a near-debt-free holding company: its earnings come from dividends, interest and its share of profits from its large stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv, so revenue (₹576 cr in H1FY27) is a small figure next to profit. Reported H1FY27 PAT fell 6.7% YoY to ₹4,845 cr and revenue fell 20.1%, but that is mainly because last year included a one-off ₹1,522 cr gain from selling Bajaj Finserv shares. Without that gain, PAT rose about 37%, and the share of associate profits grew 32% to ₹4,626 cr, helped by Bajaj Auto Q2 PAT up 62% and Bajaj Finserv up 23%. Reported growth has slowed sharply, from +65.6% to -6.7% half-year on half-year, but the underlying associate engine is accelerating. Using the holding-company yardstick (discount to NAV, not P/E or EV/EBITDA, which mean little here), the stock trades at about a 52% discount to the reported NAV of ₹21,578 per share (estimated price around ₹10,300). That sits in the middle of the usual 40–60% holdco discount band, and peer P/E of 11.4x (P33) and P/B of 1.5x with ROE of 12.6% back a 'fair' grade, with the stock in the lower third of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is concentration: value depends almost entirely on Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv share prices, and the holdco discount may not narrow, so this is a leveraged-looking proxy on two group stocks rather than an independent earnings story.

fundamental.thesis: Ambuja Cements is the Adani group's cement arm and, together with UltraTech, holds about 45% of India's cement capacity, with 109 MT of cement capacity plus an announced expansion of about 30 MTPA. Results are getting worse: Q2FY27 revenue was ₹9,197 cr and PAT ₹236 cr, a 2.6% PAT margin, down from 6.1% in Q1FY27 and about 14% in FY26. H1FY27 revenue fell 3.8% YoY and H1 PAT fell 73.8%. EBITDA per tonne slipped to ₹770 against ₹887 in FY26 and below the ₹900–1,100 healthy band, because fuel cost rose to ₹1.87 per 1,000 kcal from ₹1.60 a year ago. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive cement, the stock trades at 18.5x, in line with the Materials peer median of 17.9x (P53). The cheap-looking 22x trailing P/E and 1.7x P/B are offset by an ROE of only 8.3% and a forward P/E of 26.9x that is above trailing, which implies earnings will fall, so we grade it fair, not cheap, despite sitting near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that sell-side EPS estimates keep falling (FY down 49% in 30 days and 68% in 90 days) while imported fuel stays high and the Penna/Sanghi plants run at only about 50% utilisation. The better trade mix (74% trade share, 37% premium share) and management's guidance of higher-single-digit to double-digit volume growth in H2 are the only offsets.

fundamental.thesis: Siemens is one of India's leading electrical, automation and mobility equipment makers, with a net cash position of about ₹8,113 cr. That positions it squarely in the transmission, data-centre and rail capex cycle. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹5,734 cr, accelerating from +14.6% and +14.8% in the prior two periods, and new orders jumped 37.8% to ₹6,228 cr, with the order backlog up 12% to ₹47,034 cr (roughly 2x annualised revenue). However, PAT grew only 3.9% to ₹504 cr, an 8.8% margin, and management cites commodity and foreign-exchange pressure on material costs, with operating margin falling from 11.4% to 9.5%; Q1's 45.5% PAT margin is distorted by the one-off gain on the motors-business sale and should be ignored. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this order-book business, 52.8x is about 55% above the 34x peer median (around the 76th percentile), and trailing P/E of 76.5x sits at the top of even the 50–80x electricals band. With full-year EPS estimates cut 4.5% over 90 days, the stock looks expensive, and the biggest risk is that orders keep growing but margins don't, leaving the premium multiple to de-rate.

fundamental.thesis: Vedanta is a diversified natural-resources producer (aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, iron ore, power) that sells at global commodity prices, so it is judged on its cost position and balance sheet. Its continuing operations shrank after the demerger: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹59,872 cr, down 22.9% YoY, and Q2 revenue fell to ₹26,356 cr from ₹33,515 cr in Q1. Profit is improving even though sales are shrinking: H1 PAT rose 83% YoY to ₹9,123 cr, but Q2 PAT of ₹3,650 cr was below Q1's ₹5,473 cr, with PAT margin slipping from 16.4% to 13.8%. Prior periods were restated for the demerger, so the YoY comparisons are not clean. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, as the sector card advises for commodity names, the stock is cheap: 5.71x is the lowest of 16 Materials peers (sector median 17.9x) and at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. Forward P/E of 12.7x vs trailing 17.75x, and analysts raising FY EPS estimates by 25% over 90 days, point the same way. The main risks are that Q2 revenue and profit both fell from Q1, and that several data points don't reconcile (yfinance Q2 revenue ₹11,229 cr vs ₹26,356 cr in the filing, a 1038% dividend yield, and a 52-week range distorted by the demerger), so the inputs carry real uncertainty.

fundamental.thesis: Carborundum Universal is a mid-cap maker of abrasives, industrial ceramics and electrominerals, with a large standalone India business and overseas subsidiaries in Russia, Germany and South Africa. Revenue growth has picked up from about +2-4% YoY through FY26 to +17.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.1% in Q2FY27 (₹1,455 cr), and standalone revenue grew 28% on Ceramics (+36%). Reported Q2 PAT, however, fell 83% to ₹12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an ₹80 cr charge for closing the German subsidiary CAAG. Before exceptional items, profit (PBEBT) rose 22% to ₹138 cr, but Abrasives grew only 4% and Electrominerals profit fell 21%. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive Industrials name, the stock trades at 34.5x (P72 vs the broad market), and forward P/E is 40x (P82). The headline 115x P/E is inflated by the one-off charge. Against a 4.4% ROE and P/B of 5.8x, and with the price at 86% of its 52-week range, valuation looks expensive. Sell-side (4 sell, 2 hold) puts its mean target at roughly today's price. The biggest risk is the international subsidiaries: VAW in Russia is now on the US OFAC sanctions list, FZL in South Africa is being accounted for as not a going concern, and CAAG is winding down. Together they could bring more write-downs and keep weighing on reported earnings.

fundamental.thesis: M&M is India's dominant auto-farm conglomerate holding #1 positions across SUVs (25.3% share, +260 bps YoY), LCVs (52.3%), tractors (43.6%), and e-3-wheelers (40%), with further exposure to financial services (MMFSL), IT (TechM), real estate, and hospitality — a diversified conglomerate structure that blends cyclical and defensive earnings. Q1 FY27 delivered consolidated revenue of ₹58,188 cr (+27.8% YoY) and PAT of ₹5,455 cr (+33.6% YoY), sustaining a remarkably consistent multi-quarter growth corridor of +25–28% revenue and +33–37% PAT, with PAT margins expanding from 8.6% (FY26) to 9.4% (Q1 FY27); guidance raised twice and then maintained once signals management confidence is intact. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (appropriate for a capital-intensive OEM with a large NBFC subsidiary), M&M trades at 10.7× vs the sector peer median of 18.3×, ranking at P17 in its peer set — unambiguously cheap; trailing P/E of 19.5× is also at the lower quartile of the 18–28× Auto OEM sector range (P20 vs peers), though the stock sits at only 15.5% of its 52-week range, signalling downward momentum that could persist before fundamentals reassert. The single biggest risk is the sequential compression in the automotive PBIT margin from 9.3% in Q4FY26 to 7.7% in Q1 FY27, combined with rising crude costs (+headwind on vehicle input costs), EV mix dipping from 9.6% to 6.4% quarter-on-quarter, and a sustained RISK_OFF FII outflow environment that keeps the Auto sector on underweight — this cocktail can extend the share-price slide meaningfully before cheap valuations matter to the market.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finance is India's largest diversified retail NBFC, with AUM of ₹5,84,624 cr and a customer franchise of 128.85 million. In Q2FY27, net total income grew 23% YoY to ₹15,974 cr and PAT grew 29% to ₹6,367 cr, while AUM growth picked up from 22.4% (Q4FY26) to 24% (Q1) to 26%, and GNPA improved to 1.06% from 1.24% a year ago. Note that the trend table's Q1FY27 and H1 'revenue' rows appear to use total income rather than net income, so I rely on the like-for-like Q2 net-income figures. Using the sector card's lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock trades at 4.93x book for a 17.9% TTM ROE (20.6% annualised in Q2), the most expensive P/B among its 10 credit-services peers (P100, +62% vs the 3.0x median) and P89 on P/E at 29.6x, so it is expensive even after allowing a quality premium. The 18.3x forward P/E and the 62% dividend yield look like data errors and are not relied on. The biggest risk is that management itself guides to modest NIM moderation with up to two more repo hikes to 6%, which turns the NBFC rate tailwind into a headwind. Stage 2 and 3 assets have also risen to 2.02% from 1.87%, and the ₹17,500 cr QIP plus promoter warrants will dilute ROE in the near term.

Solar Industries makes commercial explosives for coal miners such as CIL and SCCL, and it is now growing fast as a defence ammunition and energetics supplier. It sits under the Materials label, but it is really an explosives and defence business, so steel and chemical multiples do not apply. In the half-year to September 2026 (HY27, from the official filing), revenue grew +69.7% YoY to ₹7,187 cr and PAT grew +84.3% to ₹1,316 cr. That is faster than FY26 (+30.0% revenue) and Q3FY26 (+29.0%), and defence revenue more than doubled (+109% to ₹1,935 cr). EBITDA margin widened about 140 bps to 28.4%, so the pre-computed 'contracting' margin flag looks like a period-ordering artefact. The ₹20,178 cr order book (87% defence) covers roughly 2 years of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business. At 65.8x EV/EBITDA, 101.7x trailing P/E and 32x P/B, the stock is at P93–P99 versus the broad market, well above the 12–22x Materials range and rich even for a defence name. The forward P/E of 63x and estimate upgrades (+11% FY-EPS over 90 days) show strong growth is already priced in, and the price is at 97% of its 52-week range. So: expensive. The biggest risk is that the defence order flow is lumpy and largely export-driven, so any slip in orders or execution would hit a stock priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini Mills is one of India's largest integrated sugar makers, with 80,000 TCD of cane crushing, 1,050 KLPD of distillery capacity and 175.7 MW of saleable co-generation, and it is building an 80,000 TPA PLA bioplastics plant. It is really a commodity agri-processor rather than a branded FMCG company, so the FMCG sector card's 40-60x P/E norms do not fit it. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 12.3% YoY to ₹1,876 cr and PAT rose 81.6% to ₹104 cr (PAT margin 5.5%), recovering from a weak Q1FY27 (+6.1% revenue, PAT -14.4%). Still, revenue growth has slowed from +18-22% a year ago to +9.3% for H1FY27, and EBITDA margin has fallen from 13.9% in Q3FY26 to 9.1% in Q2FY27. Because the business is capital-intensive, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: 25.0x is high for a sugar/ethanol business and sits only around the broad-market median (P56), while the trailing P/E of 38x is P55. The forward P/E of 18.5x and rising sell-side estimates (+12.7% over 90 days) already assume strong earnings growth, so on balance I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the large PLA capex (FY26 FCF of -₹349 cr) and continued margin compression fail to deliver the earnings growth the forward multiple already prices in.

fundamental.thesis: Sun Pharma is India's largest pharma company by revenue. Its earnings come from leadership in Indian branded formulations, where market share rose 0.3pp to 8.6% and formulations sales grew 16.6% in H1, and from a growing global innovative-medicines (specialty) business that is now about 21.5% of sales. H1FY27 revenue grew 11.0% YoY to ₹31,499 cr, and Q2 (₹16,315 cr, worked out as H1 minus Q1) grew 11.8%, a little faster than Q1's 10.1%. The bigger trend is slowing: growth was +15.1% in 9MFY26, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 31.9% to about 29%. Implied Q2 reported PAT of about ₹1,988 cr gives only a 12.2% margin after large Organon-acquisition and US pricing-settlement charges, and US formulations fell 8.2% in Q2 as Lenalidomide sales eroded. On the yardstick that suits a branded/specialty pharma, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E is 37.4x, inside the 28–40x sector band and at P54 among peers. Forward P/E of 27.7x (P62) and EV/EBITDA of 24.2x (13% above the peer median) leave no room for a re-rating. The biggest risk is integrating the USD 14bn Organon deal. It is several times Sun's ~₹17.7k cr net cash, so the clean balance sheet will likely take on debt, and more deal costs are flagged for coming quarters. Meanwhile sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 2.9–3.4% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: NTPC is India's largest power generator. Most of its earnings come from a regulated return (about 15.5% ROE) on the plants it has commissioned, with a fast-growing solar and renewables arm on top. H1 FY27 headline revenue was ₹100,262 cr, up 19.9% from ₹83,660 cr a year ago, but the company's core capacity-plus-energy billing grew a more modest 9.65%. Within that, capacity charges rose 6.7% to ₹35,909 cr, energy charges rose 11.6% to ₹55,845 cr and solar revenue rose 64.9% to ₹2,456 cr. Revenue growth has turned up from about -1.5% to -3% in FY26 to +7.0% in Q1 FY27 (PAT ₹6,896 cr, +12.9%, 13.6% margin), though H1 PAT was not extracted. For a capital-intensive utility I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, backed by P/B with ROE. On that basis it looks cheap against peers: EV/EBITDA is 8.4x against a peer median of 11.6x (cheapest in the peer group) and trailing P/E is 11.9x against 14.7x. P/B is 1.7x with ROE of 13.7%. It is only fair against the static 10–18x utilities P/E band. The forward P/E (12.8x) is above the trailing P/E, and this year's EPS estimates were trimmed 0.9% in the last 30 days, so near-term earnings look roughly flat. The main risk is earnings quality: CERC 2024 tariff orders are still pending, so bills are provisional and later adjusted (₹2,825 cr energy adjustment in H1), and large regulatory-deferral and deferred-tax swings make reported PAT hard to compare across periods.

fundamental.thesis: Nestle India is a leading packaged-food company (MAGGI, NESCAFE, KITKAT, infant nutrition) with deep rural and urban distribution and a premium brand franchise. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 20.5% YoY to ₹6,782 cr and PAT rose 36.3% to ₹1,027 cr (15.1% PAT margin), with double-digit volume growth reported across all product groups. Growth is slowing slightly from Q1FY27, when revenue grew 25.4% and PAT 47.9%. EBITDA margin dipped slightly to 23.8% from 24.2%, and ad spend rose 46%, so margins are not being protected by cutting brand investment. On the P/E yardstick for FMCG staples, trailing P/E of 77x sits above the sector norm of 40-65x and above the peer median of 51.5x (P83), and forward P/E of 59x is the most expensive in the sector (P100), so the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is a valuation de-rating: the current 11% volume growth is far above the company's 5-year volume CAGR of 4.2%, and the price assumes it lasts while cocoa and milk costs keep pressing on margins.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). The quality of that growth is mixed: offtake rose +7.6% to 384.2 MT while production fell -2% to 321 MT, so part of the growth came from selling down inventory, which fell 49% to 130.3 MT. Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Auto makes two- and three-wheelers and is a leading Indian exporter, with about 48% of India's two-wheeler exports and 63% of its three-wheeler exports in H1, plus a 23% Q2 market share for its Chetak electric scooter. Q2FY27 consolidated revenue rose 60% YoY to Rs 25,126 cr and PAT rose 60% to Rs 3,400 cr, but the 'accelerating' revenue signal (+19% to +32% to +60%) looks inflated by full consolidation of KTM, so unit volumes are the better guide, and their growth slowed from +29% in Q1 to +20% in Q2 while PAT margin fell from 17.1% in Q4FY26 to 14.9% and then 13.5%. Valuation is fair on the auto card's P/E yardstick, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA because the Rs 25,126 cr revenue includes low-margin consolidation effects: trailing P/E of 26.6x is inside the 18-30x OEM range and 1.9% below the 27.1x peer median (P40), while EV/EBITDA of 19.8x is 8.1% above the peer median (P67) and the stock sits at 85% of its 52-week range, which limits upside despite FY EPS estimates rising 10.3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that input-cost inflation of about 8% of revenue in H1, only about 60% recovered through pricing, continues into Q3 just as rupee support fades and rural demand weakens; some data also conflicts, including a stale-filing flag, a yfinance revenue mismatch and an implausible 145% dividend yield, so those items were not relied on.

Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% in Q1 to +20.6% (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose 225.6% to ₹5,359 cr, though the YoY figures use a low, restructured base; PAT margin was flat at about 9.8-9.9%, the 'contracting' signal is distorted by FY26's ₹18,051 cr one-off gain, and EBITDA per tonne fell about 11% QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329 despite rising 24% YoY. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a steel cyclical, the stock is expensive: the reported 12.6x, or roughly 9x on my estimate using annualised Q2 EBITDA and net debt, is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and the 13.8x trailing P/E and 'cheap vs peers' verdict carry little weight because of the one-off gain and a peer set that includes paint and adhesive companies. The biggest risk is that steel spreads narrow from here, with the stock at 92% of its 52-week range and EBITDA per tonne already falling sequentially, leaving little room for error.

Q1FY27 revenue was ₹7,043 cr (+21% YoY, accelerating from +13% in Q2FY26) with PAT of ₹581 cr (+34% YoY) and PAT margin expanding to 8.2% from 7.4% in Q1FY26 — both revenue growth and margins have moved consistently upward across six consecutive quarters. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive hospital business (per sector card guidance), Apollo trades at 33.5× vs a healthcare peer median of 23.3×, a 44% premium placing it at P75 in the sector — graded expensive, though the forward P/E of 39.1× (vs trailing 61.75×) signals meaningful earnings growth already anticipated by the market; the stock sits at 87.4% of its 52-week range, leaving limited margin of safety. Over the last four quarters revenue growth has stayed strong but bumpy (+14.8% → +45.0% → +23.0% → +31.6%), while PAT margin fell from 23.9% to 22.0% YoY because profit grew slower than sales. fundamental.thesis: Canara Bank is a large public sector bank (62.93% GoI ownership) and one of India's top-5 lenders by advances (₹13.6L cr), with a franchise spanning retail, wholesale, and treasury segments; the key yardstick here is P/B vs ROE, per the sector card, not P/E. H1FY27 shows a notable bifurcation: PAT grew strongly +31.3% YoY to ₹10,562 cr on dramatically improved asset quality (Gross NPA 1.33%, Net NPA 0.30%, PCR 95.34%), but total income contracted -3.38% YoY — revenue trajectory has decelerated from +7.7% (FY26) to -3.4% (H1FY27), driven by treasury revenue declining -18% YoY and NIM compression (2.06% FY26 vs 2.51% in Q4FY26), while PAT margin has expanded from 11.7% (FY26) to 13.1% (H1FY27) on sharply lower credit costs. At P/B of 1.02× against ROE of 15.9%, the stock is unambiguously cheap by the sector card's prescribed lender yardstick — sector card benchmark is P/B < 1.5 with ROE > 12% = cheap — and sits at P0 (cheapest) in its 14-peer regional bank cohort on both trailing P/E (6.1×, -64% vs median 16.8×) and forward P/E (5.7×), though much of this structural discount is explained by PSU overhang and below-median CASA (29.86% vs private sector ~40%+). The single biggest risk is NIM pressure persisting through the deposit repricing cycle — NIM at 2.06% for FY26 is already thin for a PSU bank and any further compression from EBLR-linked loan repricing faster than deposit cost decline would erode the PAT margin expansion thesis and keep revenue growth negative.

Lupin is a large Indian generic drug maker. It is 3rd by prescriptions in the US generics market with about a 5% share, and 8th in the Indian pharma market, where two-thirds of its domestic business is chronic therapies and its India prescription sales grew 14.4% in H1 against a market growing 14.3%. Sales are still growing but profits are not: H1 FY27 revenue rose 20.9% YoY to ₹16,104 cr (helped by the VISUfarma acquisition), while H1 PAT fell 10.9% to ₹2,638 cr. Q2 alone, worked out as H1 minus Q1, was ₹7,827 cr revenue (about +11% YoY, down from +32% in Q1) and ₹1,186 cr PAT (about -25% YoY), as the PAT margin slipped from 17.5% to roughly 15% and the pharma operating margin fell from 26.5% to 22.9%. On the EV/EBITDA yardstick used for this sector, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 19.4x against a 28–40x sector band and a 36.4x peer median (cheapest in the peer set, P0), EV/EBITDA is 12.4x (P8). Part of that discount reflects FY26 profits (+62%) that look one-off and are not repeating: forward P/E of 22.1x is above trailing P/E and analysts are cutting next-year EPS estimates (-4.5% over 90 days). The main risks are further shrinkage in US generics profits, the US review of tariffs on generics (expected within a year) and ₹5,817m of antitrust provisions still outstanding.

fundamental.thesis: Polycab is India's largest wires and cables maker, with about 30-31% share of the organised market. It is scaling a consumer electricals (FMEG) business and a smaller EPC arm, and has net cash of ₹4,520cr and an 11-day working-capital cycle. Revenue growth sped up from +39% YoY in Q1 FY27 to +53% in Q2 FY27 (₹9,900cr), and PAT rose 43% to ₹990cr. PAT margin edged up to 10.0% from 9.4% in FY26. FMEG grew 124% and posted its first double-digit EBIT margin (10.1%). Much of the headline growth is copper price pass-through, though: copper rose 40-45% in H1, while wire volumes grew only 10.5% and cable volumes about 5%. Underlying demand is healthy but well below the +53% headline. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, which suits this capital-intensive business. At 35.0x it sits close to the sector peer median of 34.0x (P53). Trailing P/E is 53.8x (P50) and forward P/E is 38.5x, which points to expected earnings growth. On the sector card's 50-80x range for electricals this is fair, not cheap, and the stock is at 99.8% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that copper-inflated revenue and record margins revert as commodity prices normalise or UltraTech's entry into wires squeezes pricing. That risk is larger because, in a risk-off market, a stock priced for perfection can lose 30-50% of its valuation multiple quickly.

The latest quarter we have read is Q1 FY27: revenue rose 13.6% YoY to ₹1,100 cr and PAT rose 12.0% to ₹837 cr. fundamental.thesis: Laurus Labs is a vertically integrated API and CDMO business with a dominant ARV generics franchise (41% of FY26 revenue) and a rapidly scaling CDMO segment (30%+ of FY26 revenue, targeting 50% by FY30) supported by 8,200 kl reactor capacity, 110 active CDMO pipeline projects, and zero critical audit findings across 132 inspections — a credible China+1 CDMO beneficiary. FY26 revenue grew +23% YoY to ₹6,813 cr with PAT up +148% YoY to ₹890 cr (PAT margin 13.1%); CDMO small-molecule delivered +38% growth and 9M CDMO grew +50%, though full-year revenue growth decelerated modestly from the +30% pace seen in 9MFY26 to +23% for the full year, while EBITDA margins expanded to 26.8% with very strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.82x FY26). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive CDMO/API model, the stock trades at 52.5x vs a sector median of 21.4x — a 145% premium — and ranks P100 (most expensive) across trailing P/E (96.6x), forward P/E (67.2x), P/B (19.8x), and EV/EBITDA in its 14-stock peer group, with the stock at 99.1% of its 52-week range: unambiguously expensive even granting a deserved CDMO re-rating premium. A ₹3,000 cr capex programme (nearly 3× the prior ₹1,000 cr guidance) must convert to contracted CDMO revenue without material slippage while the stock prices in near-flawless execution, with a pending US generics tariff review and inherent CDMO quarter-to-quarter lumpiness creating headline risk at this multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Mankind Pharma is a mainly India-focused branded drug maker, ranked #1 by prescriptions for nine straight years with a 15.2% share and limited direct exposure to US tariffs. Q2 FY27 is not reported separately in the data, but H1 less Q1 implies revenue of about Rs 4,337 cr (about +17% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 716 cr (about +38%), with quarterly revenue growth accelerating from +11.5% in Q3 FY26 to +11.8%, +12.9% and about +17%, and H1 PAT margin up 210 bps to 15.4%, backed by cash generation of 1.41x CFO/PAT. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, the stock is expensive: the listed 50.5x P/E appears to use FY26 EPS and is about 43x on my trailing-12-month estimate, still above the 28-40x sector range, while EV/EBITDA of 28.0x is 31% above the peer median (P77); I ignored the implausible 8.0% dividend yield and used net debt of 1.1x EBITDA (FY26) rather than the 38.11 debt/equity flag, which looks like a percentage. The biggest risk is that this premium assumes the Q2 jump will last, yet the source of the step-up is not visible in this data, Consumer Healthcare grew only 2.6% in H1, and FY26 volume growth was just 2.3%.

Mphasis is a mid-tier Indian IT services company. Most of its revenue comes from direct clients (98.6%), mainly in banking and insurance in the US, and its FY26 operating margin of 15.3% sat inside its 14.75–15.75% target band. The newest extracted filing is FY26, so the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been checked yet. On that older data, Q4FY26 revenue grew 7.1% YoY in constant currency and FY26 grew 6.7%, slower than the 9.5% for 9MFY26, while Q4 EPS rose 13.7% YoY. The order book looks better than revenue: deal wins (TCV) of $2.1B in FY26 were up 68%, 64% of wins were AI-led, and BFS and insurance grew 17–46%. Pipeline growth, however, slowed from 66% to 38%. Valuation is fair: trailing P/E is 24.7x, inside the 22–30x IT range and exactly at the peer median (P50). Forward P/E of 18.3x points to expected earnings growth, and the stock sits at only 30% of its 52-week range. Analysts have nudged estimates up about 1% over 30 and 90 days. The weak spot is cash: FY26 cash from operations was only 0.67x profit, and receivables days rose from 76 to 90 in a year, so profits are not fully turning into cash.

fundamental.thesis: IPCA Laboratories is a mid-sized Indian pharma maker with a chronic-therapy branded business at home (about 45% of revenue, ranked 16th in India) plus formulation and API exports through its Unichem subsidiary. Profit has risen faster than sales over the last six periods: H1 FY27 revenue grew 17.1% YoY to ₹5,698 cr and PAT jumped 50.7% to ₹814 cr, with EBITDA margin up 280 bps to 22.9%, ahead of the 22-22.3% FY27 guidance. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹2,910 cr (+14% YoY), slower than Q1's +20.8%, at a PAT margin of about 13.4%. Domestic formulations grew 13% and export formulations 33%. Using P/E with an EV/EBITDA cross-check, the stock looks fair: trailing P/E of 38x sits at the top of the 28-40x pharma range and at the 69th percentile of its peers, forward P/E is 28x and EV/EBITDA is 22.6x, about 6% above the peer median. With the price at 96% of its 52-week range and the average analyst target only about 5% above it, the earnings growth is mostly priced in.

fundamental.thesis: Exide Industries is India's largest lead-acid battery maker, covering auto OEM and replacement, home inverters, solar, industrial and export batteries, and its subsidiary EESL is building a lithium-ion cell business with a 6 GWh gigafactory commissioned on 23 Sep 2026. Growth is speeding up: H1 FY27 revenue rose 18.9% YoY to ₹10,331 cr and PAT rose 46.7% to ₹794 cr (7.7% margin). That is up from +9.4% revenue growth in Q4 FY26 and +17.7% in Q1 FY27, and EBITDA margin widened from 11.2% in FY26 to 12.2%. Taking H1 minus Q1, Q2 implies about ₹4,803 cr revenue (roughly +20% YoY) and about ₹443 cr PAT, but that figure may mix standalone and consolidated numbers, so I am not relying on it. Auto OEM sales have grown 25%+ YoY for four quarters in a row, and inverter/solar and exports are each up about 20%. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy parts maker. At 18.6x it sits slightly below the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x (P40), which makes it fair. Trailing P/E of 40.1x is well above the 18–28x auto range and in the top quartile of peers (P80), but forward P/E of 23.9x and upward EPS revisions (+6.5% over 30 days) show the market already expects strong growth, and the stock trades at 80% of its 52-week range, which limits easy upside. The biggest risk is the roughly ₹5,352 cr put into EESL so far. It is holding ROE down at 6.2%, and slow ramp-up or weak lithium-ion cell economics could keep it a drag. On top of that, management itself warns about a high base from last year's post-GST demand surge and higher input costs from crude, sulphur and a weak rupee.

fundamental.thesis: BHEL is India's dominant PSU power equipment and heavy engineering manufacturer, with leading exposure to thermal power, defence, and T&D — a direct beneficiary of the government-led capex upcycle in power and infrastructure. Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. The most critical data gap is the absence of current order-book and book-to-bill figures, which are the primary leading indicator for any capital-goods name; without these, it is impossible to confirm that the execution ramp is sustainable, and any government capex pause could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is historically prone to from near-highs.

fundamental.thesis: SRF is a diversified Indian chemicals and packaging-films maker; most of its profit comes from refrigerant gases and specialty chemicals for agrochemical and pharma clients. The SECTOR CARD places it in specialty chemicals, with the ref-gas cycle turning up. The latest quarter in the official trend table is Q1FY27, which showed revenue of ₹5,033 cr (+31.8% YoY) and PAT of ₹759 cr (+75.5% YoY), with EBITDA margin rising to 25.2% from about 18-20% through 9MFY26 and FY26 (FY26 revenue grew only +7.5%, so growth has re-accelerated sharply). However, the Q2FY27 results filed on 21 Oct are not yet in the extracted table, the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,600 cr looks inconsistent with that run-rate (likely standalone or partial), and the H1FY26 row appears mislabelled, so the newest quarter is unverified. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the card names for chemical cyclicals: 19.2x EV/EBITDA, 34.6x trailing P/E and 27.9x forward P/E sit well above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle EV/EBITDA and the 12-22x Materials P/E band, so it grades expensive. The 'cheap vs peers' verdict is not usable because the peer set is capital-goods names (ABB, CGPOWER, HAL) after a yfinance Industrials mis-tag; the stock sitting near its 52-week low (19% of range) only partly offsets this. The biggest risk is earnings quality and cycle dependence: H1 cash conversion was weak (CFO/PAT 0.63x, FCF -₹180 cr) during a heavy capex phase (₹974 cr in H1), with ₹165 cr of forex losses, so any cooling in refrigerant-gas pricing would hit a peak-margin earnings base.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Nitrite is an integrated Indian chemicals maker with a leading position in phenol and acetone (Phenolics), plus an Advanced Intermediates (AI) business serving agrochemical and other customers. Quarterly revenue growth has accelerated from +3.0% in Q3 FY26 and -3.0% in Q4 to +36.4% in Q1 FY27 and about +62% in Q2, while H1 FY27 revenue was Rs 5,654 cr (+49.0%) and PAT Rs 743 cr (+222%); Q2 is derived as H1 minus Q1 (revenue about Rs 3,076 cr, PAT about Rs 398 cr, margin about 12.9% vs 13.4% in Q1), and the gain leans on Phenolics, with H1 EBIT of Rs 933 cr, while AI margin fell to 7% from 10%. Using EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for chemical cyclicals, I grade valuation fair: the 24.6x headline (+37% vs the 17.9x peer median, P67) and 41.6x trailing P/E appear to use FY26 earnings, and my rough trailing-12-month estimates are about 14x EV/EBITDA and 22x P/E, which is below the headline but still above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle range on what may be peak earnings, while the 27.6x forward P/E implies PAT of only about Rs 830 cr, so either that figure is stale or earnings are expected to fall despite upward EPS revisions (the snapshot's dividend yield and implied price also look unreliable). The biggest risk is that Phenolics spreads normalise, as management itself signals with its 'new normal' language, just as the long-dated polycarbonate project (FY27 capex plan Rs 2,500 cr vs FY26 FCF of Rs 348 cr, commercialisation targeted by end FY2030) adds debt without near-term earnings.

fundamental.thesis: United Breweries is India's largest beer maker, owning Kingfisher and selling Heineken, with growth increasingly led by premium brands. Revenue growth improved from +10.0% in Q1 FY27 to +23.7% in Q2 FY27 (₹4,623 cr), with volumes up 16% and premium volumes up 38%, while PAT rose 190.9% to ₹135 cr from a low base of about ₹46 cr after falling 9.6% in Q1; however, the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trajectory signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly and full-year figures, and the 5.3% PAT margin appears to use net sales (about 2.9% on the listed gross revenue), against about 2.4% on the FY26 gross basis. Using the FMCG card's 40-65x P/E norm, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 84.0x is above the range and at P92 among peers, EV/EBITDA of 47.9x is at P83, and forward P/E of 46.3x is within the range but implies roughly 82% EPS growth, although the price near its 52-week low (2.6% of range) offers some sentiment support. The biggest risk is that this low-base rebound fades before earnings grow into the valuation, with next-year EPS estimates already cut 8.8% over 90 days and the ₹751.83 cr CCI penalty still before the Supreme Court; the 80% dividend yield and consensus upside figure appear to be data errors and were ignored, and the 29.08 debt/equity is likely a percentage (about 0.29x) but is unverified.

fundamental.thesis: IDBI Bank is a government- and LIC-controlled mid-size lender with a 69:31 retail-to-corporate loan mix and an unusually strong deposit base: CASA is 43.82%, well above the 35-38% sector norm, though it is down 197 bps YoY. In Q2FY27, reported total income rose only +2.8% YoY to ₹9,865 cr and PAT fell -39% to ₹2,205 cr (PAT margin 22.3% vs 62.8%), but that drop mostly reflects a ₹1,699 cr one-off NSDL stake-sale gain in Q2FY26. The underlying business is growing well: net interest income +29% to ₹4,228 cr, NIM up 40 bps YoY to 4.11%, advances +18%, deposits +17%, gross NPA down 53 bps to 2.12%, net NPA 0.17%, provision coverage 99.24% and capital adequacy 27.1%. The main risks are the NIM jump, which runs against the easing cycle, internally inconsistent prior-quarter figures (Q1 NIM shown as 2.5% while the 50 bps QoQ change implies ~3.6%), and uncertainty around the government divestment process flagged in the October 14 exchange clarification.

fundamental.thesis: L&T Finance is a large retail-focused NBFC (₹1.32 lakh crore loan book) under the L&T Group umbrella, operating across rural/farm finance, two-wheelers, housing, and consumer lending segments with strong parentage and a well-capitalised balance sheet (CAR 18.67%). Using P/B+ROE as the mandated NBFC yardstick (not P/E), LTF at 2.76× P/B with rising ROA ranks at P30 vs broad-market peers on both P/E and P/B (below sector median by 30–40%), and its trailing P/E of 24.57× sits within the 18–28× NBFC benchmark range while a forward P/E of 15.83× — a 36% discount to trailing — prices in strong near-term earnings growth, placing it at fair value with a modest cheap lean. The primary risk is that impairment provisions grew 15.6% YoY and credit cost remained elevated at 11.29% of total income, sell-side next-FY EPS estimates have been trimmed -3.2% over 30 days, and the highly leveraged balance sheet (D/E 393×) leaves LTF exposed to any funding-market stress or a slower-than-expected credit cost normalisation.

On valuation, we judged MCX as an asset-light, high-ROE exchange using P/E and EV/EBITDA rather than the P/B test used for lenders. Trailing P/E is 53.9x, forward P/E is 33.6x and EV/EBITDA is 39.3x; P/B is 17.0x with 37.9% ROE. That ranks MCX at P73–P94 against the broad market, and the stock trades only 3.3% below the average analyst target, so we rate it expensive, even though analysts raised FY-EPS estimates by 8% over 90 days and the forward P/E prices in strong growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes trading volumes stay high: if gold, silver and crude prices calm down or SEBI tightens rules, volumes could fall and the multiple could shrink quickly.

fundamental.thesis: Nippon Life India AMC is a top-5 Indian mutual fund manager with ₹7.87 trillion of MF quarterly average AUM, up 20% YoY. Its market share rose 51bps to 9.02%, led by ETFs (+135bps share gain) and B30 cities. Q2 FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹796 cr, up 21% YoY from ₹658 cr. That is in line with the +20% to +26% range of recent quarters. Reported Q2 PAT fell about 6% YoY to roughly ₹324 cr (40.7% margin), mainly because of a one-off ₹96.76 cr SEBI settlement over the AT-1 bonds, booked as an exceptional item. Market cap is about 8.6% of the ₹8.68 trillion closing AUM, with a trailing P/E of 49x and forward P/E of 35x. That is fair for a franchise compounding above 20% with a 34.5% ROE. Upside is limited, though: the stock is at 99% of its 52-week range and sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut about 5% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that AMC earnings move with equity markets. In a risk-off market with heavy FII selling, falling equity AUM and slowing SIP growth could hit revenue quickly while the stock is priced near its highs.

Niva Bupa is a standalone health insurer with about 11% of India's retail health market, 27 million lives covered and a fast-growing agent and branch network. Q2 FY27 premium grew 35% YoY to ₹2,484 cr, up from 32% in Q1, and retail health grew 47%. PAT rose 124% to ₹136 cr, a 5.5% margin, though profit was flat from Q1's ₹138 cr and the combined ratio is still very thin at 98.8% (improved from 100.2% in Q1). Valuation is graded on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for financials, because the 75x trailing P/E is distorted by a weak FY26 base: P/B of 3.84x for a 12.1% ROE looks rich, but annualised ROAN of 14.7%, a 23.5x forward P/E in line with the market median, and sell-side EPS estimates raised about 8% in the last 30 days make it fair overall. The biggest risk is that underwriting barely breaks even, so a small rise in claims inflation or a slower growth pace could quickly eat into profits that only recently improved.

fundamental.thesis: Pine Labs is India's leading merchant commerce platform operating ~2.17 million POS/DCP devices with embedded affordability finance, UPI infrastructure, and an expanding international footprint (UAE, Malaysia) — a high-growth fintech rather than a traditional lender despite its Financials sector tag. fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized, government-owned lender with gross advances of ₹2,87,690 cr. Q2FY27 net profit rose 26.8% YoY to ₹786 cr, up from +8.1% growth in Q1FY27, and asset quality kept improving: gross NPA fell from 2.56% to 1.96% and net NPA from 0.43% to 0.18% over four quarters, with provision coverage at 98.4%. Net interest income (NII) of ₹2,886 cr is about 13.9% above the year-ago revenue line of ₹2,533 cr, but that row may not be strictly NII, so treat the growth figure as approximate. For a bank we judge value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. That pressures margins as the bank pays more for deposits, and it comes in a risk-off market where foreign investors are selling financials.

Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 16.8x is 28% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P30), and forward P/E of 18.5x sits at the low end of the 18-28x auto range with estimates up 10.1% over 90 days, but the trailing P/E of 49.5x (distorted by fair-value losses) and P/B of 11.8x (P87) limit the cheapness case, and the peer set is a broad-market fallback rather than true CV peers. The biggest risk is the Iveco acquisition, whose final tender outcome, funding and integration burden are not visible in the data provided and could erode the net cash position just as the CV cycle's growth rates are guided to slow, while the auditor resignation filed on 2026-10-31 remains unexplained here.

NCC is a mid-sized Indian construction and EPC contractor (buildings, transport, water, mining, electrical) with an order book of ₹80,167 cr, about 3.9x FY26 revenue of ₹20,823 cr, so revenue visibility is solid. fundamental.thesis: R R Kabel is a mid-sized wires and cables maker with a smaller, loss-making FMEG (fans, lights, appliances) arm. Wires and cables bring in about 91% of H1 revenue (₹5,890 cr, up 54.8%), so the company rides the same power, real-estate and data-centre demand as the bigger cable makers. Growth is strong: H1 FY27 revenue rose 52.8% to ₹6,452 cr and PAT rose 87.2% to ₹386 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,284 cr (+51.8% YoY) and PAT of about ₹181 cr (+56%). That is still faster than the +19.5% of a year ago, but the Q2 PAT margin slipped to about 5.5% from 6.5% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 10.4% to roughly 9.2%. So profitability is rising year on year but has come off its Q1 peak. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick this sector card calls for, the stock trades at 32.0×, about 37% above the broad-market median (P67). Trailing P/E is 52.7× (P71) against a forward P/E of 34.0×. That multiple sits above the static 28–45× industrials P/E band, but the forward P/E and roughly 21% ROE give a fair, fully priced grade rather than a cheap one, especially with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range. There are no tight cable peers in the comparison set, so the peer rank is only broad-market context. The biggest weakness is cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.31× PAT and free cash flow was -₹159 cr. Capex of ₹280 cr in H1 pushed net debt from ₹147 cr to ₹455 cr and finance costs rose 87%. Real leverage is still modest at roughly 0.18× equity; the 13.09 debt/equity figure in the snapshot is most likely a percentage, not a multiple.

Cash conversion is less clean: FY26 free cash flow was ₹-182 cr and cash from operations was only 0.76x PAT. Because this is a commodity price-taker, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to do. At 33.4x EV/EBITDA it trades far above the 5-8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals and about 43% above the broad-market median of 23.3x. P/B of 14.8x sits at P92, so the stock looks expensive and appears to price these strong earnings as permanent, even though the 25.6x forward P/E reflects estimates that were raised 10% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that a high-copper-price year is being valued like steady growth, and Q2 FY27 results come out tomorrow (2026-11-11), so the next data point could move the view either way.

PAT growth has fallen from +88% in Q1 to roughly +28% in Q2, and the chemicals (alumina) segment is shrinking (-5.75% YoY). For a commodity price-taker the sector card says EV/EBITDA is the right measure, and 7.4x sits at the top of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. That multiple is applied to peak-cycle EBITDA margins of about 50–52%, so even though P/E is 11x (P8 vs the broad market) and analysts are raising estimates (+1.8–2.4%), the stock looks fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the record profits depend on high aluminium prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) and a weak rupee, so a commodity price reversal would compress margins quickly. Volumes are flat (Q1 metal output +0.9% YoY), so new capacity (the 5th alumina stream now, the smelter expansion later) is needed to cushion any downturn.

fundamental.thesis: GLAXO is the Indian subsidiary of GlaxoSmithKline, a premium MNC branded-formulations franchise with 22–27% market shares in general medicines and vaccines respectively, operating entirely within India's domestic market with zero US generics exposure and no tariff risk from recent US pharma levies. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated sharply to +16.56% YoY (₹938 cr vs ₹805 cr in Q1FY26), a marked re-acceleration from near-stagnation at +1.9% through FY26 and -1.2% in Q1FY26, driven by Shingrix (+65% growth), vaccines therapy (+18.5%), cardiac (+16.9%), and anti-diabetic (+17.3%) segments — PAT grew 15.68% YoY to ₹237 cr but PAT margin contracted to 25.3% from 27.1% in FY26 as S&A normalises, with management guiding EBITDA margins to settle at ~34% vs the 36-38% range seen over FY26. At a trailing P/E of 44.85× (above the 28–40× pharma sector benchmark), forward P/E of 35.72× (within range, confirming near-term earnings growth priced in), and EV/EBITDA of 33.98× (P71 vs broad market), GLAXO grades as fair — the premium is defensible for a defensive, India-only, brand-led franchise with no binary US/FDA risk, but peer rank at P65 on trailing P/E confirms there is no meaningful discount on offer. The principal risk is that the guided margin normalisation to ~34% EBITDA compresses PAT margins further if the current revenue acceleration fades back toward the guided 8–10% established-business growth range, making the present fair multiple vulnerable.
